nameStory: The Atlantic saury gets its name from its long, needle-like beak that resembles a saury sword - an old term for a thin, sharp blade. 'Saury' comes from the Greek word 'saurus' meaning lizard, referring to its elongated, reptilian-like appearance as it darts through the water.
description: The Atlantic saury is a slender, eel-like fish with a distinctive long, pointed beak lined with small teeth. These silvery fish typically grow 12-18 inches long and have a streamlined body built for speed near the ocean's surface. They're oceanic wanderers that occasionally show up in New England waters, especially during warmer months when they follow food currents closer to shore.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely elongated and slender body, almost eel-like, with a needle-sharp beak that feels hard and bony to the touch - about one-quarter the length of the entire fish

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright silvery sides that feel smooth and slippery when wet, with a darker blue-green back that has an almost metallic sheen in sunlight

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Single dorsal fin positioned far back on the body, followed by a series of small finlets between the dorsal fin and tail - these feel like tiny triangular tabs

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Long, thin beak with both jaws extended into sharp points, lined with small, needle-like teeth that feel rough when you run a finger along them

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 12-18 inches long with a pencil-thin body diameter, feeling surprisingly light and delicate for their length

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in open ocean waters near the surface, often spotted jumping or skipping across wave tops in schools during calm weather

habitat: Atlantic sauries are oceanic fish that prefer open waters well offshore from New England's coast. They're most commonly encountered in the warmer waters of the Gulf Stream or when storm systems push them closer to shore. Look for them in surface waters during calm conditions, especially around areas where currents converge and bring small prey fish together.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing in New England waters as ocean temperatures warm, often arriving with the first warm-water currents from the south.
seasonality.summer: Most abundant during peak summer months when they follow schools of small fish and plankton into nearshore waters, occasionally washing up on beaches after storms.
seasonality.fall: Start moving back to deeper, warmer offshore waters as coastal temperatures cool, though some may linger into early fall during warm years.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters, having moved to warmer southern waters or deeper ocean areas beyond the continental shelf.

funFact: Atlantic sauries can actually glide above the water's surface like flying fish! When escaping predators, they launch themselves out of the water and use their large pectoral fins to glide up to 100 feet, skipping across the waves like living javelins.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with needlefish, but sauries have their dorsal fin positioned much farther back on their body and lack the bright green bones that needlefish have. Remember: sauries are 'set back' with their fins positioned toward the tail end.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their fearsome-looking beaks, Atlantic sauries are completely harmless to humans and feed primarily on tiny plankton and small fish. Their scientific name 'Scomberesox' literally means 'mackerel pike,' reflecting their surface-dwelling lifestyle similar to mackerel but with the elongated body of a pike.
compareHints: Atlantic saury is the only member of its genus found in New England waters, making it unique among local fish. Compared to other members of the saury family worldwide, the Atlantic species is distinguished by its specific fin placement and the number of finlets behind the dorsal fin. It's most similar to needlefish in our waters, but lacks their more robust build and has a more delicate, streamlined appearance.
